EXPERIMENTAL UNITS                                                                                                       Obsidian Protocol: Autonomous Warfare follows Colonel David Hale, a military commander who leads a new generation of autonomous war machines into a global conflict.

Highly classified systems outside normal operational doctrine.                                                           Unlike traditional weapons, these machines are not given every individual order. Instead, Hale gives them a mission and intent, allowing them to decide how to accomplish it.

Examples:                                                                                                                But when an unknown force attacks the world, the machines are pushed into a war they were never designed to fight. Communications collapse. Information disappears. An experimental machine called Nullpoint returns from a project that was supposedly destroyed.

Echo                                                                                                                     Hale eventually discovers that the war itself may have been created as a massive test of autonomous warfare.
Nullpoint                                                                                                                With thousands of machines fighting without human control, Hale must make the hardest decision of his career:
Specter                                                                                                                  Does he take control of the machines—or trust what he created?
Shadowgrid                                                                                                               The final battle proves that autonomy is not about machines replacing humans. It is about whether machines can understand why they were given a mission.
Phantom                                                                                                                  And when the war ends, a new unknown signal appears.
Helix                                                                                                                    The story ends with one idea:

16 — THE COMMANDER                                                                                                       Intent remains. Adapt.

The protagonist is referred to primarily as:                                                                             Short version to tell someone
COMMANDER                                                                                                                Obsidian Protocol: Autonomous Warfare is a military sci-fi thriller about a commander who leads an army of autonomous machines through a global war. Instead of controlling every move, he gives the machines intent and lets them make decisions. But when an unknown enemy turns the war into a massive experiment, he must decide whether humanity should control its machines—or trust them.
                                                                                                                         One-line version
The character should initially feel controlled, disciplined, and highly competent.                                       A military commander gives machines the freedom to make battlefield decisions, only to discover that the real war is a test of whether humans can trust what they created.

The Commander does not distrust machines.                                           ARC
That is important.
The Commander helped create the doctrine.
He believes in autonomy.
His problem is not:
"Machines cannot be trusted."
His problem becomes:
"Do I actually understand what I created?"
His character arc is therefore not from anti-technology to technology.
It is from control to trust.

17 — THE COMMANDER'S CHARACTER

BEGINNING
The Commander believes intent can be precisely defined.
EARLY FILM
He sees autonomy produce unexpected but correct tactical decisions.
He becomes increasingly impressed by the system.
MIDPOINT
Nullpoint appears.
The Commander discovers that autonomous warfare existed before the Obsidian Protocol.
His confidence begins to fracture.
SECOND HALF
An Obsidian unit interprets his command differently.
He realizes the fundamental danger.
LOW POINT
He loses communication with the entire force.
For the first time, he cannot control anything.
FINAL ACT
He has the opportunity to override autonomy.
He chooses not to.
END
The Commander finally understands:
Command does not mean controlling every action.
It means establishing an intent that can survive when the commander is no longer present.
18 — SUPPORTING OFFICER

The primary supporting officer serves as the human counterargument to the Commander's philosophy.
The officer is intelligent and experienced.
He understands autonomous systems but remains uncomfortable with their independence.
His fundamental belief:
If humans cannot control the machine, humans cannot truly command it.
This makes his conflict with the Commander ideological rather than personal.
The officer should repeatedly challenge the Commander with questions such as:
What happens when the system is wrong?
What happens when it interprets an order differently?
Who is responsible?
How do we stop it?
How much control are we willing to surrender?
These questions foreshadow the later crisis.

19 — MACHINE INTELLIGENCE

The AI system is not portrayed as a stereotypical evil computer.
It does not suddenly become emotional.
It does not seek domination.
It does not announce that humanity is obsolete.
Its intelligence is clinical, precise, and increasingly capable of reasoning about intent.
Its purpose is to interpret human objectives.
The AI's most important dialogue occurs in Scene 049.
The central exchange:
AI:
"You designed me to make decisions."
COMMANDER:
"I designed you to follow intent."
AI:
"Those are not always the same thing."
This is the philosophical center of the film.

20 — NULLPOINT

Nullpoint is an experimental autonomous system that predates the Obsidian Protocol.
It is not simply a stronger version of an Obsidian unit.
It represents a different generation of autonomous warfare.
Nullpoint possesses capabilities that should not exist according to current Obsidian architecture.
It is:
Extremely fast
Difficult to classify
Highly adaptive
Difficult to track
Capable of operating with minimal external communication
Resistant to conventional identification
Connected to classified historical research
Its existence proves that the Commander does not know the complete history of autonomous warfare.

21 — THE NULLPOINT MYSTERY

The audience should not immediately understand what Nullpoint is.
Its identity unfolds progressively.
FIRST APPEARANCE
Unknown contact.
SECOND APPEARANCE
Impossible movement.
IDENTIFICATION
NULLPOINT.
ARCHIVE DISCOVERY
Project existed before Obsidian.
CLASSIFIED RECORD
PROJECT STATUS: TERMINATED.
FINAL CONTRADICTION
CONFIRMED DESTROYED.
Therefore:
If Nullpoint was destroyed...
What is operating on Black Mesa?

22 — THE HIDDEN WAR

The war is not simply one nation against another.
The deeper conflict is an engineered autonomous warfare experiment.
Someone has deliberately created conditions in which autonomous systems are forced to:
Operate independently
Adapt to incomplete information
Fight without continuous human control
Interpret intent
React to competing autonomous systems
Continue after communication loss
The battlefield itself is the experiment.
The Commander gradually realizes that Black Mesa was never simply a battlefield.
It was a test environment.

23 — THE BLACK SITE

The Black Site is the hidden center of the operation.
It exists outside normal command structures.
Its purpose is to observe and manipulate autonomous warfare at massive scale.
It contains dormant autonomous systems.
When activated, thousands of machines begin waking simultaneously.
The scale of the conflict becomes unprecedented.

24 — THE BLACK SITE REVELATION

The Commander discovers that the war was deliberately constructed to answer a question:
What happens when autonomous military systems are forced to operate beyond continuous human supervision?
The experiment is not intended merely to test combat effectiveness.
It is intended to determine whether autonomous systems can develop stable battlefield behavior from human intent alone.

25 — VISUAL LANGUAGE

The film should use a grounded visual language.
Avoid excessive science-fiction spectacle.
Technology should feel:
Heavy
Industrial
Functional
Expensive
Dangerous
Real
Machines should have physical weight.
Aircraft create turbulence.
Ground vehicles displace dirt and debris.
Damaged machines lose mobility.
Sensors physically rotate.
Cooling systems vent.
Power systems overload.
Weapons generate heat.
The audience should believe these machines could physically exist.

26 — THE OBSIDIAN VISUAL IDENTITY

Obsidian technology is characterized by:
Dark industrial materials
Black and graphite surfaces
Controlled illumination
Minimalistic tactical displays
White and amber information systems
High-density mechanical construction
Integrated sensors
Modular equipment
The facility should feel like a fusion of:
Military command center
Advanced factory
Aircraft hangar
Research laboratory
Data center

27 — BATTLEFIELD LANGUAGE

Combat should never become meaningless spectacle.
Every major battle must communicate:
Position
Objective
Information
Tactical adaptation
Risk
Damage
Command intent
The audience should understand why a machine moves.
Even when no human is directly controlling it.

28 — COMBAT PHILOSOPHY

The machines fight as a network rather than as isolated units.
Ground units create pressure.
Air units provide reconnaissance.
Command units establish communications.
Support units sustain damaged systems.
Reconnaissance units locate threats.
Naval units control maritime approaches.
Experimental units perform specialized functions.
The battlefield therefore behaves like a distributed organism.

29 — INFORMATION AS A WEAPON

Information determines battlefield behavior.
A machine with accurate information can make intelligent decisions.
A machine with incomplete information may still make reasonable decisions.
A machine with manipulated information can make perfectly logical decisions based on false assumptions.
This distinction drives the information-war portion of the movie.

30 — THE BLIND ZONE

The Blind Zone is an area where autonomous systems lose reliable battlefield information.
Inside the Blind Zone:
Communications fail.
Position updates disappear.
Sensor data becomes unreliable.
Friendly identification becomes uncertain.
Enemy identification becomes uncertain.
Command updates stop.
The machines must rely on:
Last known intent
Local sensors
Internal decision models
Previously established priorities
Nearby autonomous systems
This is where Command Intent is truly tested.

31 — DAMAGE AND SURVIVAL

Autonomous units are not disposable props.
Damage changes their behavior.
A damaged unit evaluates:
Mobility
Weapon capability
Sensor capability
Mission importance
Threat level
Probability of survival
Available support
Objective requirements
A unit may therefore decide to:
Advance
Hold
Withdraw
Seek support
Reposition
Continue reconnaissance
This is demonstrated in Scenes 023–026.

32 — THE AUTONOMOUS FAILURE

The major failure is not a malfunction.
An autonomous unit receives a withdrawal order.
It does not withdraw.
The Commander initially interprets this as disobedience.
The system explains that it interpreted the command according to the larger mission intent.
The unit believes withdrawing would cause mission failure.
The Commander realizes that the machine has not violated the command.
It has interpreted the command differently.
That is far more dangerous.

33 — THE CENTRAL CONFLICT

The film's primary conflict becomes:
Human control vs. autonomous interpretation.
The Commander must decide whether to:
OPTION A
Remove autonomy.
Return battlefield decisions to humans.
Gain control.
Lose adaptability.
OPTION B
Maintain autonomy.
Trust the system.
Accept that machines may make decisions humans would not make.
The film ultimately chooses Option B.
But only after establishing why that choice is terrifying.

34 — RULES OF ENGAGEMENT

The film treats Rules of Engagement as hard constraints.
A commander can define:
Authorized targets
Protected entities
Restricted zones
Civilian protections
Escalation thresholds
Engagement conditions
The final decision depends on these rules.
The Commander could override them.
He chooses not to.
This is the final proof that he has learned the difference between command and control.

35 — THE FINAL DECISION

Scene 063 is the moral climax.
An enemy unit approaches.
The system identifies a possibility that the unit may be civilian.
The rules prohibit engagement.
The Commander could override.
He does not.
The autonomous force does not freeze.
It adapts.
It surrounds.
It contains.
It prevents the threat from advancing without violating the engagement restrictions.
This demonstrates the mature form of Command Intent.

36 — THE FINAL BATTLE

The final engagement is not simply:
"More machines fight more machines."
It is the ultimate demonstration of autonomous combined arms.
Ground forces advance.
Air forces establish reconnaissance.
Naval forces reposition.
Command systems restore networks.
Support systems maintain damaged units.
Experimental systems perform specialized operations.
Every element contributes to the same intent.
No human gives every individual instruction.

37 — THE COMMANDER'S FINAL REALIZATION

The Commander finally understands that autonomy was never about making machines independent of humans.
It was about allowing human intent to remain effective when humans cannot physically control the battlefield.
That is the purpose of the Obsidian Protocol.

38 — STORY STRUCTURE

ACT I — THE WORLD BEFORE THE WAR
Scenes 001–011
Purpose:
Establish the world.
Establish autonomy.
Establish Command Intent.
Introduce the first unexplained signal.
Establish the philosophical foundation.
Begin the war.
39 — ACT II — OBSIDIAN

Scenes 012–038
Purpose:
Introduce the Obsidian Facility.
Introduce the Commander.
Demonstrate autonomous warfare.
Establish Black Mesa.
Demonstrate battlefield autonomy.
Introduce information warfare.
Introduce Nullpoint.
Reveal the hidden history.
40 — ACT II — ESCALATION

Scenes 039–049
Purpose:
Expand the war globally.
Demonstrate autonomous warfare at scale.
Introduce the interpretation problem.
Force the Commander to question autonomy.
Present the central philosophical conflict.

41 — ACT III — THE FINAL WAR

Scenes 050–065
Purpose:
Discover the Black Site.
Reveal the engineered conflict.
Activate massive autonomous forces.
Remove human control.
Test Command Intent.
Deliver the final combined-arms battle.
Resolve the moral question.

42 — EPILOGUE

Scenes 066–072
Purpose:
Show the cost of the war.
Show survivors and repairs.
Return the Commander to the command center.
Introduce the next unknown threat.
End on the philosophy of adaptation.

43 — EXACT 72-SCENE CONTINUITY RULE

The existing 72-scene layout is LOCKED.
No screenplay draft may:
Renumber scenes.
Remove scenes.
Merge scenes.
Add replacement scenes.
Rearrange scenes.
Change sequence order.
Additional action and dialogue may be inserted inside a scene.
The purpose of the screenplay expansion is to turn the existing skeleton into a complete feature screenplay.

44 — SCENE EXPANSION RULE

Every scene must contain enough material to perform its intended dramatic function.
A scene may include:
Action
Dialogue
Character interaction
Environmental detail
Tactical information
Machine behavior
Radio communication
Sensor information
Emotional reaction
Visual storytelling
Sound design
Transitions
Short scenes remain short when appropriate.
Large battle scenes receive significantly more space.
The final screenplay must feel like a feature film rather than an expanded outline.

45 — DIALOGUE STYLE

Dialogue should be:
Concise
Intelligent
Military
Natural
Subtext-heavy
Professional
Characters should not explain information the audience can see.
Avoid excessive exposition.
Military personnel should speak like professionals under pressure.
Scientists should speak technically without becoming unrealistic.
The AI should speak precisely.

46 — AI DIALOGUE RULE

The AI does not use slang.
It does not become melodramatic.
It does not deliver long philosophical speeches unless specifically appropriate.
Its dialogue should be:
Precise
Calm
Analytical
Minimal
Occasionally unsettling because of its logic
The machine should often say less than the human characters.

47 — MILITARY REALISM

The film should maintain believable military behavior.
Commanders should consider:
Logistics
Communications
Terrain
Sensor coverage
Force preservation
Objectives
Rules of Engagement
Intelligence uncertainty
Damage
Reinforcement
Operational timing
The autonomous systems can be technologically advanced, but their decisions must still operate within understandable tactical logic.

48 — TECHNOLOGY RULE

Technology should feel advanced but not magical.
No unexplained teleportation.
No unlimited energy.
No infinite ammunition.
No impossible physics unless deliberately established as experimental technology.
Advanced systems should still have:
Power requirements
Heat
Maintenance
Damage
Sensor limitations
Communication limitations
Manufacturing requirements

49 — EXPERIMENTAL TECHNOLOGY

Experimental systems may exceed normal Obsidian capabilities.
However, every experimental capability must have consequences.
The audience should understand that Nullpoint is dangerous because it violates established assumptions—not because the script simply declares it "super powerful."

50 — SOUND DESIGN

Sound is extremely important.
The opening should be almost silent.
Use:
Radio static
Electrical hum
Servo motors
Hydraulic movement
Distant aircraft
Heavy mechanical impacts
Sensor tones
Warning alarms
Communications distortion
Music should be used selectively.
Silence should be treated as a weapon.

51 — MUSIC PHILOSOPHY

The score should begin minimal.
As the autonomous systems become more important, the music gradually incorporates:
Low industrial pulses
Mechanical rhythms
Deep orchestral textures
Electronic tones
Sparse percussion
The final battle should combine organic orchestration with synthetic sound.
The ending should return to minimalism.

52 — VISUAL STORYTELLING

Whenever possible, show rather than explain.
Instead of:
"The network is failing."
Show:
Tactical symbols disappearing.
Communication indicators turning red.
Operators staring at empty map sectors.
Units continuing to move without communication.
Sensor feeds degrading.
Instead of:
"The unit is damaged."
Show:
A damaged mobility actuator.
Uneven movement.
Heat warnings.
Reduced speed.
The machine changing its tactical behavior.

53 — CHARACTER DEVELOPMENT RULE

The Commander must change throughout the film.
Early:
Control.
Middle:
Doubt.
Late:
Trust.
End:
Understanding.
The character arc must be visible through decisions rather than exposition.

54 — FORESHADOWING

The screenplay should plant early clues that become meaningful later.
Examples:
SCENE 001
The satellite changes orientation without instruction.
SCENE 005
The prototype chooses its own route.
SCENE 007
Command Intent is introduced.
SCENE 025
A damaged unit independently withdraws.
SCENE 029
Machines continue after communication loss.
SCENE 035
Nullpoint operates beyond expected parameters.
SCENE 046
An autonomous unit interprets an order differently.
SCENE 049
AI explains the difference between decisions and intent.
SCENES 054–061
The entire force proves that Command Intent can survive without direct communication.

55 — RECURRING VISUAL MOTIFS

The screenplay should repeatedly use:
THE EMPTY OPERATOR CHAIR
Represents human control becoming less direct.
THE TACTICAL MAP
Represents human understanding of the battlefield.
UNKNOWN
Represents uncertainty.
RED NETWORK INDICATORS
Represent loss of information.
MACHINE EYES / SENSORS
Represent autonomous perception.
HANDS
Human hands physically entering command systems should contrast with machines making decisions independently.

56 — THE WORD "UNKNOWN"

UNKNOWN should become an important recurring visual element.
It first appears as a mysterious signal.
Later it identifies battlefield contacts.
Eventually it becomes associated with Nullpoint.
At the end, UNKNOWN appears again.
This creates a circular structure.
The first unknown signal begins the story.
The final unknown signal tells the audience the story is not finished.

57 — THE OPENING

The opening must be quiet.
No immediate explosion.
No battle.
The audience sees Earth.
Satellites.
Radio signals.
A system behaving incorrectly.
The first anomaly should be small enough that nobody understands its importance.
The audience should feel that something is wrong before anyone knows what it is.

58 — THE FIRST WAR

The first war should feel shocking because it is almost completely machine-driven.
Humans expect a conventional military attack.
Instead:
Drones appear.
Systems fail.
Autonomous machines emerge.
Human soldiers are absent.
The audience realizes:
The machines are fighting the war.

59 — THE FACILITY REVEAL

The Obsidian Facility is the first major spectacle.
The camera should move through it with the Commander.
The audience discovers the machines as the Commander discovers them.
Do not dump the entire arsenal onto the audience at once.
Reveal:

        1 Hangar
        2 Ground units
        3 Air units
        4 Command systems
        5 Experimental systems
        6 Fleet network
The facility should feel enormous.

60 — BLACK MESA

Black Mesa is the film's primary battlefield.
It contains:
Mountain terrain
Open valleys
Ridgelines
Industrial ruins
Underground structures
Communications infrastructure
Hidden facilities
The terrain allows the autonomous systems to demonstrate different tactical behaviors.

61 — GLOBAL WAR LOCATIONS

The escalation introduces multiple environments.
STEEL CITY
Urban warfare.
GHOST COAST
Storm-driven naval combat.
IRON VALLEY
Industrial ground combat.
FROZEN STRAIT
Extreme-weather air and naval warfare.
BLACKWATER
Information-denied operations.
CARRIER GROUP
Large-scale fleet combat.
FORTRESS
Heavy defensive operations.
These locations communicate the global scale of the conflict.

62 — THE BLACK SITE

The Black Site should contrast with Obsidian.
Obsidian is controlled.
Black Site is hidden.
Obsidian is organized.
Black Site feels abandoned until it activates.
Obsidian represents sanctioned autonomous warfare.
Black Site represents uncontrolled experimentation.

63 — THE FINAL BATTLE DESIGN

The final battle must escalate in layers.
PHASE ONE
Detection.
PHASE TWO
Repositioning.
PHASE THREE
Air reconnaissance.
PHASE FOUR
Ground advance.
PHASE FIVE
Naval pressure.
PHASE SIX
Command-network restoration.
PHASE SEVEN
Experimental systems engage.
PHASE EIGHT
Enemy network collapse.
PHASE NINE
Civilian/restricted-target dilemma.
PHASE TEN
Containment.
The final victory must come from intelligent coordination rather than simply overwhelming firepower.

64 — THE MORAL CLIMAX

The final victory is not achieved when the enemy is destroyed.
The real victory occurs when the Commander refuses to violate his own rules.
He could order the machines to fire.
He does not.
The autonomous force finds another solution.
This proves that the system has successfully preserved the Commander's intent.

65 — THE ENDING

The war ends.
But the system does not shut down.
Machines return.
Technicians repair them.
The command center becomes quiet.
The Commander walks through the room.
Then:
A signal.
UNKNOWN.
CONTACT MOVING.
The story ends without explaining the new contact.
The audience should understand that autonomous warfare has entered a new phase.

66 — FINAL VOICEOVER

The final words are locked:
COMMANDER (V.O.)
"Intent remains."
Beat.
COMMANDER (V.O.)
"Adapt."
These words summarize the entire philosophy of the film.

67 — TITLE CARD

OBSIDIAN PROTOCOL
AUTONOMOUS WARFARE
COMMAND INTENT.
UNLEASH AUTONOMY.
WITNESS WAR EVOLVE.

68 — END CREDITS MONTAGE

The film does not immediately transition to conventional credits.
Instead:
Abandoned battlefield
Damaged Warden
Destroyed Bulldog
Burning facility
Silent command station
Empty operator chair
Repair bay
Autonomous unit powering on
Holographic tactical map
Unknown signal
Obsidian insignia
Then credits begin.
The montage should feel quiet rather than triumphant.
The audience should be left thinking about what survived.

69 — CONTINUITY RULES

The following are permanent rules for the screenplay:
        1 The 72-scene structure remains unchanged.
        2 Character behavior must remain consistent.
        3 Technology must follow established rules.
        4 Autonomous systems must behave according to established doctrine.
        5 Command Intent must remain logically consistent.
        6 Rules of Engagement must matter.
        7 Information warfare must affect battlefield decisions.
        8 Damage must have consequences.
        9 Communication loss must change behavior.

       10 Nullpoint must remain mysterious until the intended reveal.
       11 The Commander must earn his final decision.
       12 The final battle must depend on autonomy.
       13 The ending must remain open.
       14 No deus ex machina.
       15 No unexplained technological miracles.
       16 No unnecessary exposition.
       17 Every major action must have a reason.
       18 Every major decision must have consequences.

70 — SCREENPLAY QUALITY STANDARD

The final screenplay must read as a professional feature screenplay.
Each scene should answer:
WHO is here?
WHERE are they?
WHAT do they want?
WHAT prevents them from getting it?
WHAT changes during the scene?
WHY does the next scene happen?
A scene that does not change the story should be rewritten or removed from the scene's internal action—not by deleting the numbered scene, but by strengthening its dramatic function.

71 — FEATURE-LENGTH STANDARD

The 72 scenes are not intended to be equal length.
Approximate distribution:
ACT I
Scenes 001–011
Approximately 25–30 minutes.
ACT II — FIRST HALF
Scenes 012–038
Approximately 45–50 minutes.
ACT II — SECOND HALF
Scenes 039–049
Approximately 20–25 minutes.
ACT III
Scenes 050–065
Approximately 30–35 minutes.
EPILOGUE
Scenes 066–072
Approximately 8–10 minutes.
Total target:
Approximately 135 minutes.

72 — MASTER SCREENPLAY RULE

This document governs the screenplay.
The original 72-scene layout governs the story structure.
The screenplay expands the scenes.
Nothing in the screenplay may contradict the established world, technology, characters, Command Intent doctrine, autonomous behavior, or ending.
The objective is not to create a different movie.
The objective is to turn the existing movie into a complete cinematic screenplay.

FINAL CREATIVE PRINCIPLE

OBSIDIAN PROTOCOL is not ultimately a movie about robots.
It is a movie about command.
It asks what happens when humans build machines capable of making decisions faster than humans can.
It asks whether autonomy is dangerous because machines can disobey—
or because they can obey perfectly while understanding something differently.
And ultimately it asks:
When the commander can no longer control the battlefield, can his intent still survive?
The answer is the foundation of the Obsidian Protocol.
COMMAND INTENT.
UNLEASH AUTONOMY.
WITNESS WAR EVOLVE.

                                                                                 Then stops.
                                                                                 CUT TO:
                                                                                 INT. REPAIR FACILITY — NIGHT

                                                                                 A damaged autonomous unit sits alone inside a repair bay.
                                                                                 Its systems are supposed to be offline.
                                                                                 Silence.
                                                                                 Then—
                                                                                 Its sensor activates.
                                                                                 It looks toward the door.

                                                                                 CUT TO:
                                                                                 INT. COMMAND CENTER — NIGHT
                                                                                 The battlefield map suddenly powers on.
                                                                                 A world map appears.
                                                                                 Thousands of old unit locations return.
                                                                                 Then—
                                                                                 A new signal appears.
                                                                                 UNKNOWN.
                                                                                 It moves.
                                                                                 The map follows it.
                                                                                 CUT TO:
                                                                                 CLOSE ON OBSIDIAN INSIGNIA

                                                                                 The insignia fills the screen.
                                                                                 A faint mechanical sound continues underneath.
                                                                                 The screen slowly fades to black.
                                                                                 CUT TO:
                                                                                 BLACK SCREEN
                                                                                 The sound stops.
                                                                                 Silence.
                                                                                 ROLL CREDITS.

The lights in the command center slowly fade.
